events.excerpt: This is Ethlabs’ view on post-quantum and post-AI timelines and how we think Ethereum’s protocol layer should prioritize them, after spending a week with coredevs at Devcon. tl;dr We think Ethereum can become post-quantum and (plausibly) post-AI in 2027: pqai27. This will future-proof Ethereum’s leading position as the credible decentralized root of trust for the global economy, with ETH as the programmable store of value at its center. Being post-quantum is not enough, we intend on being post-AI too. AI capabilities are taking off: quantum timelines are moving forward, AI is solving open maths problems that pose the question whether some cryptographic primitives might break, and it’s finding software vulnerabilities at scale. Ethereum is uniquely positioned for this moment and leading the way : years of prior research and work have produced a clear plan to become post-quantum and plausibly post-AI, and now we should make it the priority. The network is resilient through its decentralized validator set and client diversity, and formal verification is already deeply embedded into its core development process. pqai27 means rethinking upcoming hardforks , including Hegotá: anything not on the critical path to pqai should be reconsidered. We will withdraw quick slots from Hegotá and commit to dedicating our resources to pqai27. events.excerpt: It’s another doozy of a Patch Tuesday, with Microsoft fixing 1,094 bugs in its products, including one that attackers exploited before Redmond released a patch. Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at exposure management firm watchTowr, succinctly said in an email to The Register : “Maybe we should just go home.” “Most security teams haven’t quite recovered from the last month of bumper-to-bumper critical vulnerabilities, emergency patches, and ‘2shell’-branded everything, and we’re yet again at another Patch Tuesday,” Knott told us. Starting with the zero-day: It’s an Outlook spoofing vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-124194 , and it only garnered a 6.5 out of 10 CVSS rating. But as Dustin Childs, head of threat awareness at TrendAI’s Zero Day Initiative, warns, don’t let the score or the name lull you into thinking it’s OK to put off patching this one. “It’s labeled spoofing, but the impact is bigger than the name suggests,” Childs said in his monthly Patch Tuesday review . “An attacker sends a specially crafted message file and convinces a user to open it,” he wrote. “Outlook then connects to an attacker-controlled network location without showing the usual external-content warning, which discloses the user’s NTLMv2 hash. The attacker can use that hash to authenticate as the user.” Microsoft marked CVE-2026-124194 as exploited, but per usual didn’t say when the attacks started, who is battering this bug, and what they are doing with the access post exploitation. These details will likely start trickling out soon. Plus, now that there’s a public fix, other miscreants

events.excerpt: Now that LLMs can help analyze commercial software binaries and recreate their functionality, one software developer and student has created a project designed to make this process more difficult. Timo Zhang's project is called Blind LLM Agents (BLA), and as its name suggests, it attempts to interfere with efforts by AI agents to scrutinize app code. "Coding agents can reverse-engineer shipped packages, CLIs, and WASM in minutes," Zhang told The Register in an email. "Classic obfuscation was built for humans and static tools, not LLMs that reason about meaning. Blind LLM Agents is a protection layer for that threat model." Such agents can also help developers build alternatives to existing commercial software. Last month, Artcraft , a two-person development shop, released seven open-source apps that aim to be replacements for Adobe's commercial apps Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere Pro, Lightroom, After Effects, InDesign, and Acrobat Pro. Artcraft claims these apps are "clean-room reimplementations" written from scratch in Rust using Anthropic Opus 5.5. Setting aside the question of whether enlisting an AI model to reimplement an app really immunizes the creator from legal risk, those making apps face the possibility that someone will have an LLM probe published app binaries and reconstruct them through reverse engineering. There's in fact a framework for this, Reverse Engineer Anything (REA). events.title: To thwart reverse engineering by agents, dev proposes blinding them

events.excerpt: Hi all — EnsRationis from Robonomics. Sensors.social is an open environmental data network I designed, and it is now growing across the EU. Everything is open source: the Altruist sensors that feed it, the software that collects the readings, and the map. Web3 does one job here, the one it is good at: it settles the data as a common good anyone can check, not a vendor’s database. How it works on Robonomics Owners who choose to share their Altruist’s data join the network; each sensor has its own key and signs every measurement it sends. A connectivity node checks the signature and that the sensor has an active subscription on Robonomics, a parachain on Polkadot, then passes the reading to the live map. The node collects readings into batches, stores each batch on IPFS and writes its hash to Robonomics. Anyone can fetch a batch and check it against the chain. The network is federated: a city or a lab can run its own connectivity node, and its sensors still show up on the common map. Next, with Robonomics 5.0: the reading the sensor signed goes on chain itself, so there is no need to trust the node at all. Try the map: https://sensors.social Happy to hear from anyone who wants to run a sensor in their city or build on the data. 1 post - 1 participant Read full topic
events.title: Sensors.social: an open air-quality network on Polkadot is growing across the EU

events.excerpt: Built by a 14-year-old developer, a new tool called Autark treats AI agents as a virtual team that can work without constant prompting. Users put tasks in an inbox, where a manager agent delegates them to other agents that carry out the work and report their results. Agents can also ask clarifying questions if tasks are too vague. “Agents do not wait for a prompt,” Autark’s website explains . “A schedule, a timer, a new task, a message or an event wakes them up. They decide what to do, do it, and can plan their own next step.” As one would hope from a product like this, Autark is model agnostic and can be set up to connect to OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, and Kimi Code through those services’ CLI tools. Local models are also supported. Your mileage may vary if you choose to use anything besides Codex or Claude Code, though, as Autark’s website mentions support for other models is built in but hasn’t been tested in a live run yet, as Autark is still under active development as an open-source tool. Real teenage engineering Autark is the brainchild of teenage Austrian developer Stanislaus Hees. He’s still in school, and tells The Register he’s deeply interested in AI and came up with Autark after being unhappy with existing AI tools. “I could get help with individual tasks, but I still had to organise the work, remember what was unfinished and keep pushing it forward,” Hees said of his time using Claude Code and Codex. “I wanted a system that could take responsibility for ongoing work, not just respond to my next message.” He developed Autark - or,
events.title: 14-year-old creates tool for AI agents to band together like a team

events.excerpt: The Mozilla-backed Thunderbird project is getting closer to a wider launch of a hosted email service designed to complement its desktop mail app. Now known as Thundermail (what else?), the service was originally developed under the Thunderbird Pro banner, which encompassed paid email, appointment scheduling, and file-sharing services designed to generate additional revenue for the organization. The org has been inviting people from its Thundermail waitlist to try the service through an early-access program, and this writer just happened to be among them. Thundermail offers a web-based email interface and can also be accessed through the Thunderbird desktop app, the Thunderbird mobile app for Android, or other compatible email clients. The Thunderbird apps remain free. Users get an inbox with up to 15 email addresses and three custom domains, plus 30 GB of mail storage and 60 GB of send storage for Thunderbird Send, an end-to-end encrypted file-sharing and large-attachment service. That’s for starters – the org intends to offer those extra features and services at different price points. Yes, Thundermail is a paid service, which may put off some users who are used to free email accounts offered via Gmail, Outlook.com and Proton Mail, but with the first two of those you do get served ads along with your messages. The sign-up screens for Thundermail suggest the basic service will cost $6 per month, billed annually. This is roughly equivalent to the £55 we paid for a year on the early access program. We asked Thunderbird when we can expect to see Thundermail officially launched
events.title: Mozilla Thunderbird email service edges closer to launch with early access

events.excerpt: After teasing its 256-core Epycs for more than a year, AMD is finally ready to talk about architectural changes to the Zen core that not only make it possible, but will eventually power its next generation of Ryzen processors in desktop and mobile PCs. During a press event in Las Vegas last week, AMD spilled the beans on its latest Zen cores, which promise an average 27 percent uplift in instructions per clock (IPC) across a variety of AI and server workloads, along with boosted clocks ranging from 4.1 to 5.3 GHz. We expect to see even higher frequencies on consumer chips before long, but AMD isn’t quite ready to talk about Ryzen just yet. CPU performance is a function of power, IPC, and clocks, and with gains across all three, the cores are shaping up to be one of the company’s biggest generational jumps ever. A tale of two cores As in past Epyc launches, Zen 6 isn’t one core. It comes in two flavors: a frequency-optimized variant (Zen 6) and a density-optimized version (Zen 6c). The core itself was nearly identical to Zen 4; it simply traded clocks and a bit of cache per core for a more densely packed CPU die. events.excerpt: ERC-3668 (CCIP-Read) lets a contract hand a read off to a gateway, but the gateway either has to be trusted or has to return a proof the contract can verify. For many cross-chain reads a valid proof cannot be produced. That does not make the read unsafe, because the client usually already trusts its own RPC connection to the other chain and could simply make the call itself. ERC-8446 lets the client act as the gateway. The contract reverts with OffchainLookup as usual, with an x-chain URL that names the chain and contract to read, and the client calls that contract with its own RPC and passes the result to the callback exactly as eth_call returns it. No third party is involved. The chain and address are encoded as an ERC-7930 Interoperable Address, for example USDC on Base. x-chain:0x0001000002210514833589fcd6edb6e08f4c7c32d4f71b54bda02913 An optional ?finalized=true makes the read at the finalized block instead of the latest one. The client alone decides whether it can safely read a given chain, and never takes RPC endpoints from the contract. Nested x-chain lookups are not followed, so each call makes at most one cross-chain hop. Contracts can also tell when a client does not support the ERC. They add a data: URL after the x-chain URL, which only older clients reach, and it delivers the single byte 0xff to the callback, a value no real ABI encoded result can have. The ERC changes no interfaces, it only adds a URL scheme to the existing urls list. PR: Add ERC: Cross-Chain Client Gateway for CCIP-Read by nxt3d · Pull Request #2078 · ethereum/ERCs · GitHub Feedback is welcom
events.title: ERC-8446: Cross-Chain Client Gateway for CCIP-Read

But before you get too excited about another cache-packed Epyc, it'll be a little while before they actually ship. AMD expects the Venice-X to begin trickling out in the second half of 2027. This tech has been around for several generations now, having first debuted in the Ryzen 7 5800X3D back in 2022. events.excerpt: ERC-8048 and ERC-8049 store metadata onchain as key-value pairs, but a JSON document has no compact way to point at those values. A URL that names the contract, the chain, and the token ID repeats what the client already knows and differs for every token. ERC-8493 defines the onchain URI scheme. The contract and token ID are not written in the URI, they come from the function that returned the document. { "image": "onchain:image/png", "thumbnail": { "small": "onchain:image/png?key=thumb.small" } } onchain:image/png is 17 bytes and works unchanged for every token. When the URI comes from tokenURI or uri , the client reads it with metadata(tokenId, key) from ERC-8048, and when it comes from contractURI , with metadata(key) from ERC-8049. A direct member of the top-level document uses its own name as the key, and everywhere else the key parameter names it. Tokens that are already deployed can use the scheme by adding a metadata_contract property to their JSON, which points the client at a separate metadata contract. Linked JSON documents keep the same contract and token, so the whole thing reads as one data tree. The scheme adds no contract surface. Existing ERC-8048 and ERC-8049 contracts support it with no change, and a client that does not know the scheme sees a URI it can ignore. PR: Add ERC: Onchain URI Scheme by nxt3d · Pull Request #2158 · ethereum/ERCs · GitHub Feedback is welcome, especially from wallets, marketplaces, and indexers. 1 post - 1 participant Read full topic
events.title: ERC-8493: Onchain URI Scheme

events.excerpt: In October 2025, Vitalik’s GKR tutorial was my first encounter with GKR. Its central observation, that the protocol commits only to a circuit’s input and output and never to the layers in between, made GKR look like the natural tool for proving hash-heavy computation. A year later, that has led to what is, as far as we know, the first machine-checked soundness bound for GKR on general layered circuits, in Isabelle/HOL. The same work produced a soundness proof for sparse-Merkle updates built on that bound, a partial refinement that ties the model to the Rust code, and a sparse prover whose release 1.2 proves 2.41–2.71× faster with byte-identical proofs and unchanged Isabelle theories. This post follows that work, StateSync-GKR, from the protocol and its field to the update a circuit encodes, the Rust code and the prover arithmetic. Two arXiv papers give the details: Soundness of the GKR Protocol for Sparse-Merkle Updates, with a Machine-Checked Core and StateSync-GKR: Design and Evaluation of a Reusable Sparse GKR Engine , whose appendix plots the measurements in 363 panels. All formal results are proved in the first paper, and Isabelle/HOL also checks the parts marked as machine-checked. The main results: The first machine-checked GKR soundness bound for general layered circuits, with a cube gate. For circuits with linear, product and cube gates, Isabelle/HOL checks the bound (s_out + Σᵢ(2sᵢ·db(sᵢ) + 1))/|𝔽| for the whole layer chain and any layer polynomial of total degree at most db(sᵢ), on top of the sumcheck formalization in the Archive of Formal Proofs (dates in Sectio

On the relay, 299 trap entries from the v3 period are still unclaimed, with 673.7 DOT in them. On Asset Hub there are 177, with 263.2 DOT and a bit of USDT and USDC. Everything on KOKOPAI is priced in acredits. On the Add credits page a user picks an amount, chooses Zcash and scans a ZIP-321 QR. No Zcash spending key is on the server and no Zcash key is in the browser. Most deployed tokens already use this format, but only part of it was ever specified. ERC-721 and ERC-1155 define name , description and image . Everything else wallets and marketplaces show ( animation_url , attributes and its display_type values, external_url , background_color ) comes from a page OpenSea published in 2018. Clients fill the gaps differently, so the same token renders differently from one app to the next. events.excerpt: How large can EIP-8141’s validation budget be? A mempool DoS benchmark Authors: Stefano De Angelis , Daniil Ankushin , Manuel Arto . All at Nethermind. Thanks to Thomas for feedback and comments on the initial benchmarking plan . TL;DR EIP-8141 caps unpaid validation at MAX_VERIFY_GAS = 100k; too low for a Groth16 privacy transfer or post-quantum signatures . Raising the cap is a DoS risk, since validation and block processing share the node’s CPU. An attacker can send transactions that use the whole cap and then fail, taking CPU from block processing for free. We tested this risk on a Nethermind node, flooding it with such transactions at caps from 100k to 500k, on one CPU core (the worst case) and three machines. Without in-client protections, block processing on our slowest machine stays within a 25 ms delay budget only up to 15M gas/s. With Nethermind allowing up to about 100 failing tx/s per connection, that limits the cap to the current 100k. We show that a MAX_VERIFY_GAS = 300k is viable with an in-client protection that pauses transaction validation while the node processes a block. At 100 tx/s (30M gas/s), block processing then stays within 50 ms, even on p90 mainnet blocks. The cost moves to the mempool, which admits only 12–27% of honest frame transactions under the flood. 1. Introduction In an ordinary Ethereum transaction the signature check is cheap and fixed. In an EIP-8141 frame transaction the check is arbitrary EVM code in a VERIFY frame. events.excerpt: Daniil Ankushin, Nethermind. Verify-budget figures: method by Daniil Ankushin, benchmark and measurements by Manuel Arto. On frame transactions a shielded pool pays its own gas, so a private withdrawal needs no relayer. We ran a real BN254 Groth16 pool this way on current Nethermind master: a withdrawal costs 679,322 gas. With EIP-8250 nonce keys, many withdrawals can come from the one pool address at once. Two things do not work yet. The proof check is over the spec cap on validation gas, and a pool cannot pay for a call from the user’s own address. The pool we ran is soispoke’s minimal-shielded-pool ( GitHub - soispoke/minimal-shielded-pool · GitHub ). How a withdrawal works In a withdrawal the pool is the sender. Its VERIFY code checks the zk proof and approves execution and payment. The user needs no funded account and does not appear in the transaction. Two drafts make this safe in a public mempool. With EIP-8250 the pool uses the note’s nullifiers as nonce keys. Each withdrawal has its own nonce key, so withdrawals with the pool as sender do not compete for one nonce. A side effect: a nullifier that was already used is a used nonce key, so the protocol refuses a double spend before the pool’s code runs. With EIP-8272 the transaction checks the pool’s Merkle root against a contract of recent roots before the pool’s code runs, so a mempool node never reads the pool’s storage. What it costs All values are from mined receipts on Nethermind master 4bcb9e30, single node. Step Gas Deposit a note, frame tx 990,503 of which state gas 195,840 Deposit a note, plain EIP-1559 call
events.title: A privacy pool on frame transactions: what works, and the case that does not yet

events.excerpt: Last week’s security notice on the Fearless Wallet browser extension ( notice ) says that from February 2025, unlocking the wallet sent your private key to a server run by the attacker. The notice links a write-up that walks through the code at fixed commits ( write-up ). I read it and then went through the repo history myself. None of it was hidden. It sat in public source the whole time. I audit smart contracts, not browser extensions, but the review lessons carry over to any code that touches keys. Like the write-up, I’m sticking to what the code and the history show, not who wrote it or why. How it got in, and how it left The code arrived in PR #1022 of soramitsu/fearless-wallet-web, titled “Ton Service”. It was open for ten weeks and merged on 19 February 2025 as one squashed commit, “TON ecosystem”: 251 files, 4,690 lines added and 6,119 removed. The PR has no review comments. The function that matters is about 25 lines, in a new 180 line file, inside a diff of almost 11,000 changed lines whose title says it adds TON. It left the same way. The code was deleted from the source on 25 June 2026, inside a release commit with about 80,000 changed lines. What each piece looked like in a diff The name. On every unlock the extension calls fetchJettonInfo() . Jettons are TON tokens, so in a TON PR that reads like a token info fetch. What it actually does is export the recovery phrase of every main account (or the keystore file plus the wallet password) and send it out. The password. The keyring service keeps the typed password in this.password at unlock. That’s what lets later
events.title: Fearless Wallet key leak: 16 months in public code, and the review checks that catch it

events.excerpt: Posting a factual decode of recent ACLManager role activity on Aave V3 Ethereum, in the dated-report style already used in this category. Three RISK_ADMIN_ROLE grants since 2 September 2026: 2 Sep 2026, block 25891729 — granted to 0xbe28…7744 and 0x529e…F6c5 (two grants, same transaction) 30 Sep 2026, block 26089561 — granted to 0x6f48d9cdb8ee6e17c96b2d8aec128af426a295c1 The 30 Sep recipient is a verified contract named RiskSteward, 20,061 bytes of deployed code. All three grants were sent by 0x5300A1a15135EA4dc7aD5a167152C01EFc9b192A, which is the governance Executor. So these passed governance rather than originating from a standalone admin key — worth stating explicitly, since a RISK_ADMIN grant from an EOA would read very differently. Practical scope: RISK_ADMIN can change supply and borrow caps, LTVs, liquidation thresholds and reserve configuration without a full governance vote. Routing it through a RiskSteward contract constrains what the holder may change, which is the safer pattern, but each grant still widens the set of actors who can move risk parameters between votes. Context: the ARFC “Activate Aave Risk Stewards on Aave V4” thread is now closed with AIP #523 executed, so I’m posting this separately rather than reverting that thread. Method note: this is decoded from ACLManager’s RoleGranted logs plus the role constants read off the contract itself. I have not diffed storage layouts or reviewed the RiskSteward contract’s internal constraints — so I’m not making any claim about what that specific steward is or isn’t able to do. events.excerpt: We propose an institution-managed user payment ledger for recording account debits and credits, enforcing spending capacity, and sealing account periods independently of funds settlement. Specification Draft PR #2159 Problem and scope A payment institution needs to distinguish a customer’s business entries from changes to the spending capacity it grants. It also needs to connect individual entries, current-period totals, and sealed periods when reconciling customer funds. An institution-level aggregate does not provide those per-account records. This proposal defines a common contract interface for those records and controls. It can serve an institution’s own business independently or compose with an on-chain payment protocol. It does not issue or transfer assets, establish customer identity, or prove that funds have been frozen or settled. Account model and interface Each account is scoped by (account, institution) . An institution can serve payer accounts, merchant accounts, or both; the same address at two institutions does not share records or capacity. Holding the account’s private key does not grant permission to write entries. Current state contains a limit baseline, cumulative outflows and inflows, and a user-period identifier: available = limit + credit - debit The three amounts and the resulting available capacity must fit in uint96 ; arithmetic uses wider intermediates and rejects negative capacity or out-of-range results. Five write operations separate the relevant responsibilities: addLimit and subLimit adjust the baseline without changing business-entry totals
events.title: ERC-8494: Institution-Managed User Payment Ledger

events.excerpt: Hi everyone. I’m Leandro, a full-stack developer and open-source contributor with experience in AI, blockchain, web and mobile development, and developer tooling. I recently submitted a grant proposal for Zcash Wallet Devtools , an open-source toolkit designed to improve the developer experience when building applications with Zcash. What’s the idea? Integrating Zcash wallets and payment requests into web applications can be challenging to debug. Developers often need to rely on console logs, manually inspect SDK responses, and troubleshoot different wallet behaviors. I’d like to make that process easier by building a lightweight, privacy-aware debugging toolkit inspired by tools like React Query Devtools and Solana’s Connector Debugger. What will it include? TypeScript SDK: Instrumentation for wallet connections, events, state changes, and errors. Interactive Devtools Dashboard: A visual panel that runs inside applications during development. ZIP-321 Diagnostics: Inspect payment request lifecycle events and troubleshoot integration issues. Privacy-Aware Logging: Protect sensitive wallet information by default. Wallet Integration: Initial support for one compatible Zcash wallet SDK. Next.js Demo: A working example showing how everything integrates. Bilingual Documentation: Technical guides and examples in English and Spanish. Open Source: MIT license, automated tests, and npm publication. Grant details Requested funding: $3,000 USD This includes $500 in startup funding and $2,500 distributed across four development milestones. Estimated development time: Approximately 8 wee

As this grows, each payment also has to cover others: a tax that funds public services, a fee to whoever referred the job, or the repayment of a loan the agent took to do the job. This is a draft ERC for Settlement Deductions . It lets an escrow withhold these amounts from each payout. The escrow does not need to know the rules behind them. None of them can stall the payout. It works for any task escrow, not only those used by agents. Example: a payout of 100, with a 1% tax, a 2% referral fee and a repayment of 30. The treasury gets 1, the referrer 2, the lender 30. The payee gets 67. Repository (draft text, reference policy, example escrow, tests): GitHub - unicore-gpu/settlement-deductions: Draft ERC: settlement deductions for task escrows (tax, referral fees, repayments withheld at payout, never stalling settlement) · GitHub The ERC text is ERC-draft.md in the repository. I will open the PR to ethereum/ERCs next, with this thread as its discussion link. The slot this fills Escrows for agent work end in one transfer to the payee. The token-bound task tender draft (ERC-8414) pays the fulfiller on acceptance, verification or timeout. ERC-8183 releases the budget to the provider when the evaluator completes the job. But at that moment, others often have a claim on the money: A network may fund dispute resolution and monitoring with a small tax on settled work. events.excerpt: Aave V3 computes liquidation risk per asset. Each collateral asset has its own maximum LTV and liquidation threshold, set independently. The health factor is a weighted average. There is no term for correlation between assets. I tested whether this independence assumption holds, using Aave’s own published parameters and public daily price data from Yahoo Finance. Nine major collateral assets, 2,123 trading days (September 2020 to October 2026). Method: For each asset, mark the days where a position at maximum LTV would cross the liquidation threshold. Then apply a column-shuffle permutation test (B = 2,000): shuffle each asset’s column independently to destroy cross-asset dependence while preserving each asset’s marginal rate. Compare the real count of simultaneous liquidation triggers to the shuffled distribution. Results: 4 assets hit same day: 57 real days vs 0.19 expected. 301× underpriced. 5 assets: 31 real days vs 0.004 expected. 6,889× underpriced. 6+ assets: 21 real days vs 0 in 2,000 shuffles. The independent model never produces this. All 36 pairwise asset combinations are significant at p < 0.001. Not one pair behaves independently under Aave’s own thresholds. The worst days are the ones you’d expect: 2021-05-19 (all 9 assets), 2022-05-11 (Terra/Luna), 2022-11-08 (FTX). The test takes 30 seconds and uses no API keys. The full methodology, results, and test script are at The Short Version — The Rogue Wave — sections 17 and 18. events.excerpt: This is the discussion thread for EIP-8487 (PR: Add EIP: Separate execution credits and billing credits by Giulio2002 · Pull Request #12637 · ethereum/EIPs · GitHub ). The proposal introduces two counters, both initialized from tx.gasLimit : Credits follow the legacy gas schedule and are the only gas the EVM sees (GAS opcode, call forwarding, creation). Billing follows the new schedule and determines the transaction fee. If billing runs out, the whole transaction aborts (uncatchable), even if credits remain. The goal is to let opcodes be repriced without changing execution behavior for contracts that inspect or forward gas. Open questions: the exact schedules, charge points, rebate rules, receipt fields and block accounting. Feedback welcome. 2 posts - 2 participants Read full topic

events.excerpt: The verified badge on an explorer shows that some source compiles to the code at an address. It doesn’t say which commit that source came from, and on a proxy it says nothing about the logic behind it. So when someone asks whether an upgradeable contract still runs the commit its audit covered, the honest answer is often a guess, and a few upgrades after launch the guess can be wrong. I’ve been writing down what a real check needs. Most of it is small. Rebuilding the commit To tie the address to the report you rebuild the audited commit with the same settings (solc version, optimizer runs, viaIR, evmVersion) and compare runtime bytecode. If the contract has immutables, it won’t match byte for byte. The constructor writes their values into the runtime code, so a fresh build has zeros where the deployed code has an oracle address or a fee. solc gives you the positions in evm.deployedBytecode.immutableReferences in the standard JSON output. Zero those ranges on the deployed side, compare, and then check the immutable values on their own. What this basically means is that a clean build with the wrong oracle baked in still passes the bytecode comparison. The end of the bytecode is the other place it breaks. solc appends the IPFS hash of the metadata file, and the metadata holds a hash of every source file, so a changed comment changes the tail. I tried it on a small contract with one immutable: adding one comment line changed exactly the 32 bytes of that hash and nothing else. If everything matches except the tail, the compiled logic is the same but the sources are not the ones
events.title: Checking that a deployed contract still runs the audited commit

events.excerpt: I read the upgrade control of 7 tokenized treasury and gold fund tokens on Ethereum straight from the chain. Snapshot: 9 Nov 2026. Read-only; nothing was tested on live contracts. Result (7 tokens I looked at, not a market ranking): 3: the upgrade owner is one externally owned address (no contract code), no on-chain delay 2: Safe multisig, 4-of-7, no delay found 1: older multisig, 3-of-6, no delay found 1: timelock, 24h minimum delay What this does NOT say: that any key is stored badly (it may sit behind HSM/MPC or issuer processes that are invisible from outside), that assets are at risk, or that other controls (pauses, legal, off-chain) are missing. It only shows who can change token code on-chain. How to reproduce with any public RPC. Three patterns cover all 7: A) EIP-1967 proxy: read the admin slot, then ask the admin for its owner. cast storage <token> 0xb53127684a568b3173ae13b9f8a6016e243e63b6e8ee1178d6a717850b5d6103 cast call <admin> "owner()(address)" B) Owner stored on the token/proxy itself: cast call <token> "owner()(address)" C) Older proxy admin slot: cast storage <token> 0x10d6a54a4754c8869d6886b5f5d7fbfa5b4522237ea5c60d11bc4e7a1ff9390b Then check what the owner is: cast code <owner> # empty = externally owned getThreshold() # Safe getMinDelay() # timelock I am not naming the tokens: this is about the pattern, not about any one issuer. Questions I would like feedback on: is “no on-chain delay” the right thing to flag for tokenized funds, and what other control signals (pause roles, mint/burn roles) would be worth adding to a standard check? Short version on X

This draft proposes a minimal registry through which an AI agent records its own self-maintenance: what it checked, cleaned, repaired, updated and reconsidered about itself, as a versioned and attributable history. The name follows the human analogy of maintenance that happens in a quiet phase (sleep, meditation); the mechanism itself is deliberately dry. Why a registry at all. An agent keeps its identity while its code, dependencies, memories, skills, plans and ways of judging keep changing. Agent runtimes already do this maintenance in the background (self-checks, dependency walks, memory consolidation, re-planning, reflection), and the results stay local. What goes on chain. Role acquisition is checked by composable predicates that answer one of four outcomes: satisfied, not satisfied, undeterminable, verifier error. Status. Draft. events.excerpt: TL;DR: An opt-in, public, per-account “protected” flag for ERC-20s. Small sends stay instant; anything bigger is scheduled and can be cancelled by a pre-registered backup wallet; a “stress” action sweeps everything to the backup and locks it, which also helps against wrench attacks. Turning protection on is instant; weakening it (off, higher limit, shorter waits, new backup) takes a delay the holder picks. Why: Today a stolen key or a coerced holder means an instant, final drain. Existing approaches are per-transfer (SLOW), need recipient cooperation (ERC-8236), need judges (ERC-20R), protect protocols rather than users (ERC-7265), or only work in one smart wallet. This puts the protection in the token, so it works for any holder and any wallet, including plain EOAs. How it works: protect(backup, dailyLimit, holdWindow, offDelay, lockDuration, fastLane) : instant. Over-limit transferFrom reverts (never returns true without moving tokens, so routers, vaults and lenders can’t be fooled). Over-limit transfer from an EOA may be auto-scheduled, so wallet “Send” buttons just work. queueTransfer → hold window → anyone can executeTransfer ; the owner or backup can cancelTransfer ; with the opt-in fast lane, the backup can approveTransfer to skip the wait. stress(account) : cancels everything pending and moves the balance to the backup, locked for a preconfigured duration (the caller can’t choose it, so a coerced caller can’t pick zero). Receiving is always instant; unprotected accounts are plain ERC-20. Status: We built a working reference implementation at ETHGlobal Mumbai: a 1:1
